stories.headline: The Darkest Day in the History of Jammu & Kashmir
stories.title: The Darkest Day in the History of Jammu & Kashmir
stories.summary: CROSS ROADS No single event has shaped the uncertainty of the future that the people of Jammu & Kashmir (J&K) uncomfortably and hesitantly peek out towards than those that unfolded on 22 October 1947. In the din of the cacophony of voices parroting ad nauseam terms such as the Line of Control (LoC), the United Nations (UN) Resolutions on J&K, the Shimla Agreement, statehood for Gilgit Baltistan, Article 370 of India’s Constitution, and the like, the reason why these terms came into being in the first place has sadly long ceased to be a matter of interest to a vast majority of even those that deliberate publicly and vociferously on the plight of J&K. On that very day the seeds were sown for the physical tearing apart of J&K, for what we see today as the blurring of the identity of J&K and its people, for the destruction of the peaceful and inclusive way of life in the region and the crumbling of the long-held social values in J&K, and for the induction of the ugly head of terrorism into J&K by Pakistan. In essence, the roots of the hydra-headed predicament that J&K confronts today can indubitably be traced back to that one single event that commenced on that fateful autumn day. As gripping and intriguing as the history of the region in the period leading up to, and in the aftermath of, the events of October 1947 were, for the purpose of this piece, I shall restrict it to sketching the broad outlines. Maharaja Hari Singh, the Hindu Dogra ruler of Muslim-majority J&K at the time of India’s independence, seemed inclined towards independence and did not initially appear to be keen to join either dominion. On 12 August 1947, he therefore sought a standstill agreement with both India and Pakistan. He communicated to both that the “Jammu and Kashmir government would welcome standstill agreement with Union of India/Pakistan on all matters on which there exists arrangements with the outgoing British India government”. India responded by asking Maharaja Hari Singh to send his representative to Delhi for further discussions. J&K did not send a representative to Delhi, and no negotiations were consequently held. Pakistan, on the other hand, accepted the J&K offer of a standstill agreement and on 15 August 1947 sent a communication to Janak Singh, the then Prime Minister of J&K, confirming the same. Pakistan, however, made its nefarious designs on J&K clear when within 12 days of agreeing to the standstill agreement, on 24 August 1947 it threatened Maharaja Hari Singh by writing to him that “The time has come for Maharaja of Kashmir that he must take his choice and choose Pakistan. Should Kashmir fail to join Pakistan, the gravest possible trouble will inevitably ensue”. These turned out to be ominous words indeed, as from that day onwards and continuing onto the present day, Pakistan’s consistent policy has actually been to incessantly and ruthlessly stir up the “gravest possible trouble” in J&K. By end-August 1947, suspecting that Maharaja Hari Singh may accede to India and apprehensive of the popular J&K leader Sheikh Abdullah’s dim view of Pakistan, Pakistan had already decided to seize J&K by force. The then Pakistani military officer in charge of Kashmir, Major General Akbar Khan, had aptly summarized the thinking in the Pakistani establishment when he wrote, “Kashmir’s accession to Pakistan was not simply a matter of desirability but of absolute necessity for its separate existence”. On 4 September 1947, General Henry Lawrence Scott, commander of the Jammu and Kashmir State forces, complained about multiple covert incursions from Pakistan and asked the Maharaja’s government to raise this issue with Pakistan. In his autobiography, Dr. Karan Singh, the son of Maharaja Hari Singh and the heir apparent of J&K, wrote, “Intelligence reports from the frontier areas of Poonch and Mirpur as well as the Sialkot sector started coming in which spoke of large-scale massacre, loot and rape of our villagers by aggressive hordes from across the borders. I recall the grim atmosphere that began to engulf us as it gradually became clear that we were losing control of the outer areas”. Operation Gulmarg had been conceived and put into action as early as on 20 August 1947, just six days after Pakistan was carved out from British India. The plan, as openly reported since, was for Pashtun tribes of Pakistan’s North-West Frontier Province (NWFP) to enlist at least one Lashkar of 1000 tribesmen each. Separate instructions for their recruitment were issued to the Deputy Commissioners and Political Agents of NWFP. After enlistment, these Lashkars were to be concentrated at Bannu, Wana, Peshawar, Kohat, Thal and Nowshera by the first week of September 1947. The Pakistan Army Brigade Commanders at these places were to issue them arms and ammunition. The Pakistani Army superimposed a Pathan Major, a Captain and ten JCOs of the regular Pakistan Army above each such armed Lashkar, and these Army regulars were required to dress and live exactly like the other Pathans in the Lashkar. The entire force was commanded by Major General Akbar Khan, code named General Tariq, who was assisted by Brigadier Sher Khan. Among those who planned, led, and financed Operation Gulmarg, the most prominent was Sardar Shaukat Hayat Khan, a close confidant of Pakistan’s founder Muhammad Ali Jinnah and a top leader of the Muslim League. In his book ‘The Nation that Lost its Soul’, Shaukat Hayat Khan acknowledged that he had been appointed supervisor of the Kashmir operation (P.278), and that Major Khurshid Anwar was given the responsibility of contacting the chiefs of the Pathan tribes to enlist the tribal militants. He also disclosed that three hundred thousand rupees were given from the Pakistan treasury by Finance Minister Ghulam Muhammad for this operation. Major General Akbar Khan fixed 22 October 1947 as the date on which the attack on J&K would be launched. All the Lashkars were asked to converge at Abbottabad near the border with J&K by 18 October. They were moved in civil buses and trucks that had been commandeered for this purpose, and all their movement took place under the cover of night. The tribal militants assembled in a separate area 16 km outside Abbottabad that had been prepared for them. Infantry Divisions of the Pakistani Army also descended on the Murree-Abbottabad and other key areas with instructions to move in quickly into J&K to back up the Lashkars and consolidate their hold over captured territory. Operation Gulmarg was launched on the intervening night of 21-22 October 1947. Over 2,000 Pathan tribesmen first captured the bridge spanning the Kishanganga (Neelam) River on the Hazara Trunk Road linking Muzaffarabad with Abbottabad without a fight. The J&K troops guarding the bridge deserted and joined the attacking tribesmen. By morning, the first major J&K border town of Muzaffarabad had been captured. The horrors that then unfolded in Muzaffarabad were chronicled by Pakistani journalist Zahid Chaudhry in his 12-volume work 'Pakistan ki siyasi tarikh' (Political History of Pakistan). Chaudhry wrote that for three days the invaders indulged in killing non-Muslims, looting, plundering and burning their houses. A large number of women were raped and kidnapped. As the officer in-charge of the attack, Major Khurshid Anwar encouraged the killing, loot, arson, rape and kidnapping of non-Muslims that took place. Writers and commentators have estimated the number of the Hindus and Sikhs massacred during these three days in Muzaffarabad to be 4500 to 5000, and the number of kidnapped women to be more than 1600. Pakistan has perpetuated the myth that the tribal raiders were liberators and came to Kashmir to fulfil their religious obligation of Jihad because Muslims were being killed in Jammu in communal riots. However, the reality was that it was not as if Muslims had been spared. Thousands of Kashmiri Muslims were also killed by the marauding tribesmen. As an eyewitness account of Khawaja Abdul Samad asserted, “their attack had totally devastated Muzaffarabad, the homes of Hindus and Muslims were looted, shops were plundered, places of worships were not spared; they tore down Mandirs and desecrated Masjids”. Zahid Chaudhry pointed out that the Afridi and Mahsud Lashkars did not participate in the invasion of J&K out of any religious consideration, and their primary aim was loot and plunder and the kidnapping of women. Gohar Rahman of Battagram, 80 km north-west of Garhi Habibullah in Pakistan, who had participated in the invasion and had returned to Garhi Habibullah along with many other tribesmen when the first winter snows came, later told the BBC that the tribal militants had “returned with war booty”. He elaborated that “Some had brought cattle, some horses. Most of them had brought arms, and many brought women. One Afridi tribesman walked back with two women in tow. They wept incessantly and just wouldn't stop”. The Pakistan Army then directed the Lashkars to Mirpur, after capturing which they moved on to take Uri before reaching the vibrant and important town of Baramulla, about 50 kms west of Srinagar, on 26 October. The mayhem of killings, rapes and plunder was repeated at every stop along the route, while other Lashkars that had been sent through other routes with different targets in J&K did not account for themselves any better. Baramulla, however, represented another major town that bore the brunt of the ruthless ways of the tribal militants. On 26 October 1947 alone, the intruders massacred about eleven thousand residents of Baramulla and destroyed the Mohra power station. Estimates of the total number of residents of J&K killed in the tribal invasion range between 35,000 to 40,000. The march of the tribal Lashkars forward to Srinagar got stalled in Baramulla on 27 October for three days. Sardar Shaukat Hayat Khan revealed that the tribal Lashkars refused to listen to Major Khurshid Anwar when they arrived in Baramulla. They demanded the three hundred thousand rupees that they believed was meant for them. Major Khurshid Anwar refused, saying that the amount had been given for the whole operation. This angered the tribesmen, who started indiscriminate looting and plundering not only in the town but all over the entire district. Whatever be the reason, historians agree that the delay of three days at Baramulla decided the fate of Kashmir invasion. The ease with which the Lashkars overran the thin and ill-prepared troops of J&K in Uri and Baramulla, the massive massacre of 26 October 1947 in Baramulla, and with the fall of Srinagar looking imminent, the panic-stricken Maharaja Hari Singh appealed to India to come to his rescue. He wrote in a letter dated 26 October 1947, “With the conditions obtaining at present in my State and to great emergency of the situation as it exists, I have no option but to ask for help from the Indian Dominion. Naturally they cannot send the help asked for by me without my State acceding to the Domination of India. I have accordingly decided to do so and I attach the Instrument of Accession for acceptance by your Government. The other alternative is to leave my State and my people to diabolical killers and beasts. On this basis, no civilized Government can exist or be maintained. The alternative I will never allow to happen as long as I am Ruler of the State and I have life to defend my country”. With J&K formally and legally acceding to India, Indian troops landed in Srinagar on 27 October 1947 and defended the summer capital in the decisive battle of Shalteng on the outskirts of Srinagar on 7-8 November 1947. The decorated Indian commander Brigadier L.P. Sen recaptured Baramulla on the morning of 8 November, and his troops marched down the Jhelum gorge to recapture Uri. The Indian Army then liberated the long-besieged Poonch garrison and pushed the Lashkars back, and also made substantial gains on other fronts. Over the next few months, they drove out the Pakistani intruders from most parts of J&K, barring the portion that today constitutes Pakistan Occupied J&K. The invasion of J&K by Pakistan and its proxy tribal Lashkars in 1947 has left a deep, lasting, and grim mark on the fate of J&K, and indeed of the entire South Asian region. The horrors of the violence left deep scars that impacted the psyche of the people of J&K, and it marked the first and most critical step in the erosion of the Kashmiri identity with the State and its people being torn apart by a UN-drawn LoC that divides the erstwhile Princely State and its inhabitants. For those in J&K and India, as also in the international community, that buy into the Pakistani propaganda of it being genuinely concerned about the welfare of its “Muslim brethren” in J&K, it is important to realize that the Pakistani policy first adopted in October 1947 of attempting to grab J&K by force has dealt the greatest blow possible to the existence of a unified State of J&K, to the essence of what it means to be a Kashmiri, and to the prospects for the economic progress and prosperity of the people of J&K. The planners and perpetuators of the tribal invasion were, and remain, without doubt the foremost enemies of the Kashmiri people. The day the invasion began on 22 October 1947, similarly, has to be the darkest day in the history of J&K. (The Author is the Director of the European Foundation for South Asian Studies (EFSAS) and can be reached at j.qureshi@efsas.org )

stories.headline: Market sell-off deepens as midcaps enter correction zone
stories.title: Market sell-off deepens as midcaps enter correction zone
stories.summary: Mumbai: The recent sell-off in Indian equities has pushed the Nifty Midcap 150 index into correction territory, with small-cap and micro-cap indices not far behind.The Nifty Midcap 150 has fallen 10.2% from its 52-week high recorded on August 31, after declining 1.4% on Wednesday. The Nifty Smallcap 250 index has dropped 8% from its September 8 high, following a 2.3% fall during the day.The Nifty Microcap 250 index is down 8.1% from its recent high in the first week of October after tumbling 2.6%. The Sensex and Nifty, which ended around 0.5% lower each on Wednesday, have declined nearly 15% so far in 2026.Although there is no universally accepted definition of a market correction, a decline of 10% or more, but less than 20%, from a recent high is generally considered one.135103453Many smaller stocks have broadly withstood the weak sentiment in the market and sharp declines in blue chips over the past two years thanks to a flood of retail money through equity mutual funds and directly. But concerns over elevated valuations are beginning to catch up as investors evaluate whether the broader risk-off sentiment could impact future returns.Over the past two years, the midcap and smallcap indices have each entered correction territory three times. The midcap index fell nearly 19% from its January 2025 high to its February low. The smallcap index fell nearly 26% in this period, entering bear market territory but subsequently recovered.Read more: Sundaram Mutual Fund announces launch of Equity Ex-Top 100 Long Short Fund through its SIF platform SelectAnand Radhakrishnan, managing director of Sundaram Mutual, said some domestic investors had shifted money from large-cap stocks to mid-cap and smallcaps, viewing them as safe amid foreign investors' selling. This perception could be slowly shifting with valuations rising."What is perceived as a safe space can gradually become unsafe as valuations go up. We are seeing corrections even in midcap and smallcap stocks, although this may not yet be visible at the index level," he said.Read more: Jio IPO Day 1: Issue subscribed 3 times on strong QIB push; retail portion booked 68%. Check GMPOf the 97 stocks in the midcap index that have hit 52-week highs so far in 2026, two have fallen 40-45% from their peaks, 18 have declined 30-40%, 35 have lost 20-30%, and 42 are down 1-20%.In the smallcap segment, 172 stocks have hit 52-week highs so far this year. Of these, nine have declined 40-45% from their peaks, 32 have fallen 30-40%, 54 have lost 20-30%, and 77 are down 1-20%.In the microcap segment, 165 stocks have hit 52-week highs this year. Of these, seven have fallen 40-50%, 23 have declined 30-40%, 64 have lost 20-30%, and 70 are down 1-20%.Even after the recent declines, valuations are still at a premium over large-caps. The mid-cap index is currently trading at a 42% premium to the Nifty, compared with its five-year average of 40%. The small-cap index is trading at a 45% premium, below its five-year average of 75%, analysts said."Small and mid-cap valuations have come off from very high levels but remain on the higher side," said Atul Bhole, executive vice-president and fund manager at Kotak Mahindra AMC. "That said, the aggregate earnings outlook is holding up very well, with 16-20% earnings growth projected for the midcap and smallcap universe. Any improvement in news flows on the war, crude prices and yields could cause a relief rally."

opening: Mumbai: The recent sell-off in Indian equities has pushed the Nifty Midcap 150 index into correction territory, with small-cap and micro-cap indices not far behind.
The Nifty Midcap 150 has fallen 10.2% from its 52-week high recorded on August 31, after declining 1.4% on Wednesday.
body: Although there is no universally accepted definition of a market correction, a decline of 10% or more, but less than 20%, from a recent high is generally considered one.

Many smaller stocks have broadly withstood the weak sentiment in the market and sharp declines in blue chips over the past two years thanks to a flood of retail money through equity mutual funds and directly.
But concerns over elevated valuations are beginning to catch up as investors evaluate whether the broader risk-off sentiment could impact future returns.
Over the past two years, the midcap and smallcap indices have each entered correction territory three times.
The smallcap index fell nearly 26% in this period, entering bear market territory but subsequently recovered.

Sundaram Mutual Fund announces launch of Equity Ex-Top 100 Long Short Fund through its SIF platform SelectAnand Radhakrishnan, managing director of Sundaram Mutual, said some domestic investors had shifted money from large-cap stocks to mid-cap and smallcaps, viewing them as safe amid foreign investors' selling.
This perception could be slowly shifting with valuations rising." What is perceived as a safe space can gradually become unsafe as valuations go up.
We are seeing corrections even in midcap and smallcap stocks, although this may not yet be visible at the index level," he said.
Jio IPO Day 1: Issue subscribed 3 times on strong QIB push; retail portion booked 68%.
In the smallcap segment, 172 stocks have hit 52-week highs so far this year.
Of these, nine have declined 40-45% from their peaks, 32 have fallen 30-40%, 54 have lost 20-30%, and 77 are down 1-20%.
In the microcap segment, 165 stocks have hit 52-week highs this year.
Of these, seven have fallen 40-50%, 23 have declined 30-40%, 64 have lost 20-30%, and 70 are down 1-20%.
Even after the recent declines, valuations are still at a premium over large-caps.
The mid-cap index is currently trading at a 42% premium to the Nifty, compared with its five-year average of 40%.

stories.headline: LG Ladakh notifies amendment in record 6 days, council seats rationalised
stories.title: LG Ladakh notifies amendment in record 6 days, council seats rationalised
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 21: Ladakh is all set to hold elections to eight Autonomous Hill Development Councils after President Droupadi Murmu promulgated the Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Councils (LAHDC) (Amendment) Regulation, 2026. Lieutenant Governor Vinai Kumar Saxena notified the regulation with effect from October 19, terming it a “historic regulation”. Officials said the regulation was implemented in a record time of just six days. The Union Cabinet approved the amendments on October 14, followed by promulgation by the President on October 16. The regulation paves the way for creation of LAHDC in all eight districts of Ladakh, including the newly created Sankoo district. Ladakh earlier had only two hill councils — in Leh and Kargil, before the administration created five new districts including Sham, Nubra, Changthang, Zanskar and Drass in April and Sankoo on October 16. The amended regulation rationalises the number of constituencies from the earlier fixed 26 seats in each council to a minimum of seven seats and a maximum of 24 seats. It also provides for nomination of four members from ‘women’ and ‘unrepresented communities’ for greater people’s participation. Powers to conduct the polls have been assigned to the State Election Commission (SEC), which will be responsible for superintendence, direction and control of elections and preparation of electoral rolls. The regulation also substitutes the word ‘Governor’ with ‘Administrator’ throughout the LAHDC Act, 1997, defining Administrator as the Administrator of UT Ladakh appointed by the President under Article 239. “I am pleased to announce that upon the promulgation of the Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Councils (Amendment) Regulation, 2026, by the Hon’ble President of India, I have notified the regulation with effect from 19 October 2026. The historic regulation, implemented in a record time of just six days, now paves the way for creation of LAHDC in all 8 districts of Ladakh, including the newly created Sankoo district,” LG Ladakh posted on ‘X’. “The Union Cabinet had approved the amendments on 14 October, followed by its promulgation by the Hon’ble President on 16th October” LG Ladakh said. LG said that the amended regulation rationalises the number of constituencies – from the earlier 26 seats in each Council, to a minimum of 7 seats and maximum 24 seats now. It also provides for nomination of four members from “women” and “unrepresented communities” for greater people’s participation in the local governance. LG Saxena thanked Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah for the “landmark regulation, that will strengthen grassroots democracy, enhance local representation and promote inclusivity”. However, leaders of the Leh Apex Body (LAB) and Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA), which are spearheading agitation for constitutional safeguards and statehood, have opposed the amendment alleging that hill council powers have been curtailed and UT administration’s control strengthened. Under the new provisions, councils will exercise district-level Panchayat powers, while district plans will have to adhere to administrative guidelines and their bye-laws will require approval from the administration.

stories.headline: Ladakh makes judicial history
stories.title: Ladakh makes judicial history
stories.summary: Leh, Oct 21: A historic chapter in the Indian judicial history unfolded on Wednesday when Chief Justice of the High Court of J&K and Ladakh, Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Sanjay Parihar presided over the first regular division bench at Leh. The newly established Ladakh Bench of the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh located at a breath-taking height of over 11,500 feet above sea level, began regular hearing of the cases from Wednesday. The day began with the hearing by the Division Bench in which the Chief Justice heard the matters through virtual mode while Justice Sanjay Parihar was present physically at the Ladakh Bench. After the conclusion of the hearing of five listed Division Bench matters, Justice Sanjay Parihar sat singly and dealt with as many as 60 matters listed before the single bench. Today’s proceedings made use of technology to facilitate a sort of hybrid hearing with the Chief Justice hearing through virtual mode and Justice Sanjay Parihar doing physical hearing. Justice Parihar said that the identification of the 65 cases that were listed today reflects the initial effort to organise and facilitate the hearing of matters concerning litigants from Ladakh. He said that the successful commencement of regular judicial hearings today by the Chief Justice in such a high-altitude location is a landmark achievement in the country’s judicial infrastructure and commitment to ensuring that geographical barriers do not become obstacles to justice. The establishment of the Ladakh Bench is a significant step in strengthening the reach of constitutional institutions to remote and geographically challenging regions of the country. Earlier, litigants from Leh, Kargil, and other far-flung areas of Ladakh would undertake lengthy journeys to Srinagar or Jammu for proceedings before the High Court. The commencement of hearings here is also encouraging for the legal fraternity of Ladakh including advocates. Ladakh Bench of J& K High court was formally inaugurated by the Chief Justice of India Justice Surya Kant on October 18 at Melongthang, Leh.

stories.title: Kerala landslide derails express train, Amrit Bharat among services hit
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: A landslide near Parassala railway station derailed a locomotive in Kerala, disrupting nine other trains, including the Amrit Bharat Express.
Check details.

A landslide near Parassala railway station in Kerala’s Thiruvananthapuram district derailed the locomotive of the Bilaspur-Tirunelveli Express early Thursday, disrupting services on the Neyyattinkara-Parassala section.
The disruption affected several other trains, including the Tambaram-Thiruvananthapuram Central Amrit Bharat Express.
The incident occurred at 2.19 am when Train No. 22619, the Bilaspur-Tirunelveli Express, was stopped near Parassala following the landslide.
The locomotive was subsequently found to have derailed, Southern Railway said.
All passengers and railway staff are safe, according to the railway authorities.
Three trains were held en route following the incident.
The Tambaram-Thiruvananthapuram Central Special was stopped at Eraniel, the Madurai-Punalur Express at North Panakudi and the Tambaram-Thiruvananthapuram Central Amrit Bharat Express at Nanguneri.
- The Guruvayur-Chennai Egmore Express and the Pune-Kanniyakumari Express were also expected to face delays, Southern Railway said.
Railway authorities arranged a relief locomotive to move the stranded train.
An accident relief train, along with personnel and equipment, was also sent to the site to carry out restoration work and resume services.

stories.headline: CRPF pays homage to martyrs on Police Commemoration Day at GC Humhama
stories.title: CRPF pays homage to martyrs on Police Commemoration Day at GC Humhama
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 21: Ten valiant CRPF personnel laid down their lives in an ambush laid by heavily armed Chinese troops at Hot Springs, Ladakh on October 21, 1959. October 21 is observed in commemoration of these martyrs and all other police personnel who attained martyrdom in the line of duty. The Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) solemnly observed Police Commemoration Day on Wednesday at Group Centre (GC), Humhama, Srinagar, to pay heartfelt tributes to the brave police personnel who made the supreme sacrifice in the line of duty while safeguarding the nation. The commemorative programme was presided over by Sh. Rajesh Kumar, IPS, Special Director General (SDG), J&K Zone, CRPF, and was attended by Sh. Pawan Kumar Sharma, IG, Srinagar Sector; Sh. Vivek Bhandral, DIG; Sh. Praveen Kumar Singh, DIG; Sh. Harvinder Singh Kales, DIG; Smt. Swapna G. Meshram, IPS, DIG; and other officers and personnel of the Force. The programme commenced with the SDG, J&K Zone, laying a wreath at the Martyrs’ Memorial, paying solemn homage to the brave hearts who laid down their lives in the service of the nation. The gathering observed the occasion with deep reverence, remembering the courage, dedication and supreme sacrifices of the martyrs. Addressing the officers and personnel present on the occasion, the SDG, J&K Zone, highlighted the significance of Police Commemoration Day and paid tribute to the unwavering commitment and valour of police personnel who made the ultimate sacrifice in the line of duty. As part of the solemn ceremony, the SDG, J&K Zone, read out the names of all 154 police personnel who attained martyrdom during 2026, honouring their selfless service and supreme sacrifice. The ceremony served as a poignant reminder of the Force’s rich legacy of courage, sacrifice and devotion to duty. The programme also included a ceremonial ‘Salami Shastra’ at the Quarter Guard, reflecting the Force’s deep respect for its martyrs and its enduring tradition of discipline and honour. The observance concluded with a renewed pledge by Force personnel to uphold the highest traditions of the CRPF and continue serving the nation with courage, integrity and dedication. The occasion reaffirmed the Force’s commitment to honouring the memory of its martyrs and carrying forward their legacy of selfless service to the nation. Besides, commemorative roll calls and memorial gatherings were also organised across CRPF units and formations across the country to pay tribute to the martyrs. The Union Home Minister also acknowledged the sacrifices of police personnel in safeguarding the country’s borders, sovereignty and internal security while addressing the gathering at the National Police Memorial, New Delhi.

stories.headline: Srinagar’s Sprawl is No Mark of Progress
stories.title: Srinagar’s Sprawl is No Mark of Progress
stories.summary: Srinagar is expanding, but it is not growing in the manner a city should. Its boundaries are spreading into villages, agricultural fields, wetlands and open spaces without a coherent urban vision to guide that transformation. What is being celebrated as development increasingly resembles uncontrolled sprawl—a disorderly outward march that is placing immense pressure on land, infrastructure and the environment. The city’s expansion is visible along every major approach road. New colonies, commercial structures and residential complexes are rising rapidly on the outskirts, often ahead of roads, drainage systems, public transport, schools and healthcare facilities. In several areas, construction has become the first sign of urban planning; civic services arrive later, if they arrive at all. This reverses the basic logic of responsible development. Srinagar’s geography makes such expansion particularly dangerous. The city is surrounded by wetlands, water channels, orchards and agricultural land that perform essential ecological functions. These spaces absorb excess water, moderate temperatures and sustain livelihoods. When they are filled, narrowed or built over, the consequences are not limited to the loss of scenery. Flooding becomes more severe, traffic congestion spreads, groundwater systems are disturbed and the city’s capacity to withstand extreme weather declines. The recurring expansion of built-up areas also exposes the weakness of enforcement. Master plans and zoning regulations have little meaning if violations are regularised after construction or if permissions are granted without assessing the cumulative impact on roads, drainage and public utilities. A city cannot be planned plot by plot while ignoring the combined pressure created by thousands of new structures. Urban sprawl also deepens inequality. Affluent developments may create private access roads and independent services, while ordinary residents in peripheral colonies are left with inadequate transport, poor waste collection, unreliable drainage and limited public amenities. The result is a city that becomes larger but not more liveable. Srinagar urgently needs a transparent and enforceable urban growth strategy. Construction on wetlands, flood channels and prime agricultural land must face strict scrutiny. Public transport and compact, mixed-use development should be prioritised over endless low-density expansion. Local bodies must be equipped with updated maps, technical staff and the authority to act against illegal construction—regardless of influence. The question is not whether Srinagar should develop. It must. The question is whether development will serve the city or slowly destroy the conditions that make it habitable. If urban growth continues without ecological restraint and civic planning, Srinagar will inherit the worst features of a metropolis without gaining the benefits of one. Progress cannot mean covering every available piece of land with concrete. A liveable Srinagar must be planned before it is permitted to spread beyond repair.

The result is a city that becomes larger but not more liveable.
Srinagar urgently needs a transparent and enforceable urban growth strategy.
Construction on wetlands, flood channels and prime agricultural land must face strict scrutiny.
Public transport and compact, mixed-use development should be prioritised over endless low-density expansion.
Local bodies must be equipped with updated maps, technical staff and the authority to act against illegal construction—regardless of influence.
The question is not whether Srinagar should develop.
It must.
The question is whether development will serve the city or slowly destroy the conditions that make it habitable.
If urban growth continues without ecological restraint and civic planning, Srinagar will inherit the worst features of a metropolis without gaining the benefits of one.
Progress cannot mean covering every available piece of land with concrete.
A liveable Srinagar must be planned before it is permitted to spread beyond repair.

stories.headline: Div Com reviews alignment of Srinagar Ring Road Phase-III, Parimpora–Dalgate Flyover
stories.title: Div Com reviews alignment of Srinagar Ring Road Phase-III, Parimpora–Dalgate Flyover
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 21: Divisional Commissioner Kashmir, Anshul Garg on Wednesday chaired a meeting of officers to review the cahnge in proposed realignments of Srinagar Ring Road Phase-III (Lasjan–Pandach) and the Parimpora–Dalgate Flyover. The meeting was attended by the Commissioner, Srinagar Municipal Corporation (SMC); Deputy Commissioner Srinagar; SSP Traffic; Vice Chairman, Lakes Conservation and Management Authority (LCMA); Project Director, National Highways Authority of India (NHAI); and officers from the Roads and Buildings (R&B) Department, Irrigation and Flood Control Department, Srinagar Development Authority (SDA), and other concerned departments. During the review of Srinagar Ring Road Phase-III (Lasjan–Pandach), the Divisional Commissioner directed NHAI officials to compile comprehensive details of structures and departmental utilities falling within the proposed alignments including religious structures to access impediments & challenges and cost expenditure. He further directed the concerned authorities to explore modifications to the alignment to ensure that the road does not encroach upon the city's major water body. Reviewing the proposed alignment of the Parimpora–Dalgate Flyover, the Divisional Commissioner directed the R&B Department to explore an alternative alignments from Qamarwari to Nalamar and onward to Karanagar. He emphasized the need to ensure connectivity to key facilities, including SMHS Hospital, while minimizing traffic disruptions during the execution of the project. The concerned departments were directed to examine the proposed alignments in coordination with one another, keeping public convenience and essential infrastructure.
